hook: Python OOP is **lighter than C#** — fewer keywords, more conventions. Six ideas, no fluff.

scenes.title: class is the same. **self** is the difference.
scenes.sub: The instance passes itself to every method
scenes.narration: A Python class looks familiar — class keyword, methods inside. The big difference: every instance method takes self as its first parameter, and you pass it explicitly. Self is this — but visible. The constructor is a dunder method called init. No access modifiers either: one underscore means 'please don't', two means 'name-mangled, really don't' — it's convention, not enforcement.

items.s: Attributes are created by assignment — no field declarations

scenes.narration: Mechanics: init runs at construction. Attributes just appear when you assign them — no declaration block, no types required. And privacy is by honor: underscore prefix says 'internal', double underscore makes the compiler rename it so subclasses can't collide. Python trusts you more than C sharp does — that includes trusting you not to break things.

scenes.title: **Dunder** = the interface protocol
scenes.narration: Dunder means double underscore. These methods plug your class into Python's own syntax. Implement len and len of your object works. Implement eq and double-equals works. Implement str and print shows something human. It's C sharp's operator overloading plus interfaces plus ToString — one mechanism, everywhere, no ceremony.

items.s: Also makes your object pass truthiness checks naturally

scenes.narration: The ones you'll write constantly: len for length, str for display, repr for debugging, eq for value comparison. Add getitem and square-bracket indexing works on your object. The mindset shift: you're not calling methods, you're teaching Python's operators what your object means. This is exactly how Pydantic models behave like plain data.

scenes.title: Inheritance exists. **Prefer composition.**
scenes.sub: super() calls the parent — mixins are common
scenes.narration: Inheritance works as you'd expect: class B of A, super calls the parent, and you can override or extend. But Python's culture is blunter than C sharp's: deep hierarchies are frowned on. Composition and duck typing solve most problems inheritance used to. When you do inherit, keep it shallow — one level, maybe two.

items.s: Inherit, override run(), call super().run() to extend behavior
Python 3: plain super() inside a method — no class name needed
class JsonMixin, class LoggerMixin — composed, not deep trees

scenes.narration: Syntax: class Tool, parenthesis Base Tool. Super with empty parens calls the parent — cleaner than C sharp's base keyword. And a Python specialty: mixins — tiny classes that add one capability, composed together. Agent frameworks love them: one mixin for logging, one for retries, one for schema — stack them, stay flat.

scenes.title: dataclass = **record type**, built in
scenes.narration: Here's the class you'll actually write most. Put at-dataclass above a class, list fields with type hints, and Python generates the constructor, equality, and a clean repr automatically. It's C sharp's record types — constructor, equality, ToString — with one decorator. Defaults, mutable defaults done safely, even frozen for immutability.

items.s: Three lines replace fifteen — init, eq, repr generated
Immutable records — hashable, safe to share
Safe mutable defaults — the trap from Reel 4, handled for you

scenes.narration: The essentials: at-dataclass, then fields as class annotations with defaults. Frozen equals true makes it immutable — perfect for config and value objects. And field with default factory creates fresh mutable values per instance — the mutable-default trap, solved by design. When you outgrow dataclasses, Pydantic models are the next step — that's Reel 9.

scenes.title: Interfaces: **Protocol beats ABC**
scenes.sub: Duck typing + static checking = structural interfaces
scenes.narration: C sharp interfaces are nominal — you declare them. Python has two options. Abstract base classes: the C sharp way, explicit inheritance. Protocols: the modern way — you define the methods you expect, and any class that happens to implement them automatically satisfies the protocol. No inheritance needed. It's structural typing, exactly like TypeScript.

cards.s: class Storage(ABC) + @abstractmethod. Explicit, but forces inheritance.
class Storage(Protocol): def save(...) — any match qualifies. Zero coupling.

scenes.narration: Side by side. ABC: you inherit from it, and forget a method — instantiation fails loudly. Protocol: you just declare the shape, and mypy checks that anything passed in matches. Your vector store, your cache, your LLM client — define them as protocols and test doubles become trivial. In 2026 codebases, reach for Protocol first.

scenes.title: Methods that behave like **fields**
scenes.narration: Last tool: property turns a method into an attribute. Access it without parentheses, but it computes on every read. This is where validation and derived values live: a temperature in Celsius that also exposes Fahrenheit, or a config that reads an environment variable lazily. Pair it with a setter and you get C sharp property syntax, Python-style.

items.s: model.cost_usd — no parens, computed fresh each read
Raise ValueError on bad input — validation lives in the class
Compute once, then serve the cached value forever

scenes.narration: The pattern: at-property for computed reads, at-name dot setter for guarded writes. ValueError on anything invalid — fail fast, close to the data. And when the computation is expensive but stable, cached property from functools computes once and memoizes. Clean, testable, and no boilerplate getters in sight.

scenes.title: From scripts to a real project
scenes.next: Reel 6 · Modules & Project Structure — imports, layout, entry points

recap: self is explicit; attributes are created by assignment; _underscore = convention
Dunders plug your class into Python syntax; dataclasses replace boilerplate records
Protocol > ABC for interfaces; @property = computed fields

quiz.q: What does the `@dataclass` decorator generate for you?
quiz.why: @dataclass reads the type-annotated fields and generates the constructor, equality, and repr — C# record types in one line.

quiz.q: What's the key difference between ABC and Protocol?
opts: Protocol uses structural typing — any class with the right methods matches, no inheritance
quiz.why: ABC is nominal (explicit inheritance); Protocol is structural (duck typing checked by mypy) — zero coupling, like TypeScript interfaces.
__len__ plugs your class into len(); same pattern: __str__ → print, __eq__ → ==, __getitem__ → obj[i].

code.title: OOP the Python way — 30 lines, everything from this reel
annot: frozen=True → immutable + hashable; still allows @property computed values
Protocol + mypy: pass ANY object with save/load — test doubles are one-liners
Method chaining (`return self`) is idiomatic for builders like this Pipeline

notes:
# OOP in Python

## Classes & __init__
```python
class Model:
    def __init__(self, name: str, price: float = 0.0):
        self.name = name          # attribute created by assignment
        self.price = price
```
- `self` = C# `this`, but explicit in every method signature.
- `_x` = internal by convention · `__x` = name-mangled (not truly private).

## Dunder methods
| Dunder | Enables |
| --- | --- |
| `__init__` | construction |
| `__len__` | `len(obj)` |
| `__str__` / `__repr__` | `print` / REPL debug |
| `__eq__` | `==` |
| `__getitem__` | `obj[i]` |

## Inheritance & super()
- `class Tool(BaseTool):` · `super().run()` (Py3: bare `super()`).
- **Keep hierarchies shallow** — prefer composition + mixins.

## dataclasses
```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Model:
    name: str
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)
```
= records: `__init__` + `__eq__` + `__repr__` generated.

## Protocol & ABC
- **ABC**: nominal — inherit, `@abstractmethod`, loud failures.
- **Protocol**: structural — declare the shape; any match qualifies (mypy-checked). Prefer Protocol.

## @property
- Computed attribute without `()`; add `@x.setter` for validation; `functools.cached_property` to memoize.
